reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase), resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation; it is classified as glycogen storage disease type II
It is unusual among the glycogenoses in being a lysosomal disorder rather than affecting cytoplasmic glycogen metabolism, so fasting hypoglycaemia is not a feature
The classic infantile form presents in the first months with profound hypotonia, a rapidly enlarging heart (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and feeding and respiratory difficulty
A markedly enlarged tongue and prominent cardiomegaly on chest imaging are useful clues in infants
Late-onset (juvenile and adult) forms present with progressive proximal and respiratory muscle weakness and often lack significant cardiac involvement
Diaphragmatic weakness can cause respiratory failure that is disproportionate to limb weakness
Serum creatine kinase is commonly elevated, reflecting the underlying myopathy
Enzyme replacement therapy has transformed the outlook, particularly in infantile disease, and newborn screening enables earlier treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Pompe disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the GAA gene encoding acid alpha-glucosidase, the lysosomal enzyme that degrades glycogen to glucose within the lysosome. Deficient activity leads to progressive lysosomal glycogen accumulation, most damaging in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Lysosomal engorgement and subsequent autophagic dysfunction impair muscle architecture and function, producing cardiomegaly and hypotonia in infants and progressive skeletal and respiratory muscle weakness in later-onset disease. The degree of residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with age of onset and severity.
additionalDifferentials: Spinal muscular atrophy and other causes of infantile hypotonia
Congenital muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies
Other causes of infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies in later-onset presentations
Other glycogen storage disorders affecting muscle
additionalInvestigations: Assay of acid alpha-glucosidase activity, including dried blood spot screening with confirmatory testing
Echocardiography and ECG to assess cardiomyopathy in infants
Pulmonary function testing and muscle assessment in later-onset disease
redFlags: Rapidly progressive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in an infant
Severe feeding difficulty with failure to thrive
Progressive respiratory decline out of proportion to limb weakness in older patients
reference.prognosis: Untreated classic infantile disease is usually fatal within the first year from cardiorespiratory failure. Enzyme replacement therapy substantially improves survival and cardiac outcomes, especially when started early, though respiratory and motor sequelae may persist. Late-onset disease progresses more slowly, with respiratory function being a key determinant of long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Expecting hypoglycaemia and being misled when it is absent, since this is a lysosomal rather than cytoplasmic glycogenosis
Attributing infantile hypotonia to a neuromuscular cause without checking for cardiomyopathy
Underestimating respiratory muscle involvement in later-onset disease
Delaying treatment when early initiation most influences outcome
management: Enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant acid alpha-glucosidase (alglucosidase alfa or avalglucosidase alfa) as the disease-specific mainstay, started as early as possible in infantile disease
Immune tolerance induction with agents such as rituximab, methotrexate and immunoglobulin in CRIM-negative infants to limit neutralising anti-enzyme antibodies
Respiratory support for diaphragmatic and respiratory muscle weakness, including non-invasive or invasive ventilation and airway clearance
Cardiac monitoring and heart-failure management for the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of the infantile form
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and mobility aids, with dietetic support and safe-swallow measures for feeding difficulty
Regular surveillance of respiratory function, motor status, cardiac status and anti-enzyme antibody titres
Metabolic medicine-led multidisciplinary care with genetic counselling and family testing for autosomal recessive inheritance
